one_liner: comma.ai's shared-memory ring-buffer pub/sub for one machine, callable from Python and C++; about 3.2x pyzmq IPC on Python-driven ping-pong.
what_it_does: msgq passes byte messages between processes on the same host. Each named endpoint has exactly one publisher and up to 25 subscribers. The Python API is pub_sock/sub_sock with send(), receive() (blocking, non-blocking or with a timeout), conflate=True to keep only the latest message, a Poller for several subscribers, and wait_for_readers(). The C++ API has the same shape (PubSocket/SubSocket/Poller in msgq/ipc.h) over a small C-style core in msgq/msgq.h. It is not a ZeroMQ drop-in: there are no transports other than local shared memory, no REQ/REP or PUSH/PULL, and no multi-publisher topics. The repo also ships VisionIPC for camera buffers and a fake backend for deterministic tests.
how_it_is_fast: Each endpoint is a file in /dev/shm that every process mmaps. It holds a header of 64-bit atomics, each packing a 32-bit wrap-cycle counter with a 32-bit offset, one for the writer and one per reader, followed by a single-producer, multi-consumer byte ring of 8-byte-size-prefixed records. A send is a memcpy into the ring plus an atomic write-pointer update, then a tkill(SIGUSR2) to each reader thread to interrupt its nanosleep-based poll. A receive is a memcpy out, bracketed by checks of a per-reader validity flag in the style of a seqlock optimistic read, so there are no locks and no kernel socket copies. The writer never waits for readers: readers it laps are invalidated and reset, so there is no backpressure work on the hot path.
when_to_use: Same-host sensor or telemetry pipelines where Python and C/C++ processes publish and subscribe to the same topics (openpilot's use case).
Latest-value streams where dropping stale messages is acceptable or wanted; conflate=True returns only the newest message.
Small to medium messages (64 B to 64 KiB are exercised by the benchmark) at high rates, where per-message syscalls and kernel copies (Unix sockets, pipes) cost too much CPU.
Linux on x86-64 or aarch64 with /dev/shm, using CPython 3.11 to 3.14 (prebuilt manylinux, musllinux and macOS wheels on PyPI as msgq-ipc).
Tests that need to step a pub/sub system deterministically, via the bundled fake backend (CEREAL_FAKE).
when_not_to_use: Any cross-host messaging: there is no network transport, and the subscriber address must be 127.0.0.1 (enforced by assert).
Workloads that need reliable delivery, backpressure, acknowledgements or persistence: a slow subscriber is silently reset to the write head and loses messages.
Topics with several producers, or request/reply and fan-in patterns: a new publisher takes over the endpoint and the old one's send fails with MultiplePublishersError.
More than 25 subscribers on one topic, or messages larger than a third of the segment (about 349 KB with the default 1 MiB segment) unless segment_size is raised.
Latency-sensitive work on macOS, which has no tkill and polls every 10 ms instead; processes that already use SIGUSR2; containers without a shared /dev/shm.

integration.form: module (pip wheel msgq-ipc with Cython bindings); static libs libmsgq.a / libvisionipc.a via SCons for C++
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (librt on Linux); build needs SCons, Cython>=3.1 and setuptools>=77
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (CI and wheels); macOS x86-64/arm64 wheels, where wake-ups fall back to 10 ms polling
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The code has no locks. A random per-publisher UID enforces a single writer and reader slots are claimed by CAS, but each socket object holds unsynchronized state, so sharing one socket across threads is at your own risk.

gotchas: Despite folklore calling it zero-copy, the README says it copies on both send and receive. Large frames go through VisionIPC instead.

Hard limits are enforced with assert(), and the SCons build does not define NDEBUG. A message over segment/3 aborts the publisher, and an empty message trips the receiver's size>0 assert. A 26th subscriber evicts every reader on the endpoint, which then re-registers (open issue #702 calls the fixed cap a footgun).

Creating a queue installs a SIGUSR2 handler, and every send signals each subscriber's thread. The signal targets the thread that created the subscriber, so receiving on another thread waits out the poll timeout (100 ms slices when blocking). A rare lost wake-up in poll is acknowledged in closed issue #208.

Creating a publisher resets the endpoint's reader table, so create publishers before subscribers (the benchmark barriers on this). Queue files in /dev/shm are never unlinked. OPENPILOT_PREFIX namespaces them.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick msgq over Monocoque (ZeroMQ-style REQ/REP over IPC and TCP) or TCPSHM (point-to-point TCP/SHM round trips) when you need one-to-many same-host pub/sub that Python and C++ can both use, and lossy latest-value delivery is fine. Choose those siblings or Zenoh when you need request/reply, reliable delivery or a network hop.
verified_claims_summary: The README's chart comes from msgq/examples/benchmark.py: two Python processes play 1 KiB ping-pong on an unspecified x86 Linux machine, taking the median of 5 randomized repeats. msgq reached 362.13k msgs/s against 113.97k for pyzmq XPUB/SUB over ipc:// (about 3.2x), with multiprocessing.Pipe at 231.66k, LCM UDP at 173.68k and Zenoh over a Unix socket at 86.03k. Counting both directions, that is about 181k round trips/s, or roughly 5.5 us per round trip including Python overhead. This is not native libzmq, no CPU, kernel or compiler is given (the SCons build uses -O2), and the 64 B and 64 KiB runs are not published.
status_note: Actively maintained: v1.0 went to PyPI as msgq-ipc in September 2026, the last commit was 2026-09-09, and it runs in production in openpilot as a git submodule. It is MIT-licensed, and its roughly 500-line C++ core is easy to vendor, but the packaging depends on SCons and Cython.
